source_text: Τότε τοίνυν αἴθριοι διανυκτερεύειν κατεδικάσθησαν, ὅτε λίμνη μὲν, περὶ ἣν ἡ πόλις κατῴκισται, ἐν ᾗ ταῦτα διήθλουν οἱ ἅγιοι, οἷόν τι πεδίον ἱππήλατον ἦν, μεταποιήσαντος αὐτὴν τοῦ κρυστάλλου· καὶ ἠπειρωθεῖσα τῷ κρύει, ἀσφαλῶς ὑπὲρ νῶτον πεζεύειν παρείχετο τοῖς περιοίκοις· ποταμοὶ δὲ ἀένναα ῥέοντες, τῷ κρυστάλλῳ δεθέντες, τῶν ῥείθρων ἔστησαν· ἥ τε ἁπαλὴ τοῦ ὕδατος φύσις πρὸς τὴν τῶν λίθων ἀντιτυπίαν μετεποιήθη· βορέου δὲ δριμεῖαι πνοαὶ τὸ ἔμψυχον ἅπαν ἐπὶ τὸν θάνατον ἤπειγον. Τότε τοίνυν ἀκούσαντες τοῦ προστάγματος (καὶ σκόπει μοι ἐνταῦθα τῶν ἀνδρῶν τὸ ἀήττητον), με τὰ χαρᾶς ἀποῤῥίψαντες ἕκαστος καὶ τὸν τελευταῖον χιτῶνα, πρὸς τὸν διὰ τοῦ κρύους ἐχώρουν θάνατον, ὥσπερ ἐν σκύλων διαρπαγῇ ἀλλήλοις ἐγκελευόμενοι. Μὴ γὰρ ἱμάτιον, φησὶν, ἀποδυόμεθα, ἀλλὰ τὸν πα λαιὸν ἄνθρωπον ἀποτιθέμεθα, τὸν φθειρόμενον κατὰ τὰς ἐπιθυμίας τῆς ἀπάτης. Εὐχαριστοῦμέν σοι, Κύριε, τῷ ἱματίῳ τούτῳ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν συναποβάλ λοντες. Ἐπειδὴ διὰ τὸν ὄφιν ἐνεδυσάμεθα, διὰ τὸν Χριστὸν ἐκδυσώμεθα. Μὴ ἀντισχώμεθα ἱματίων διὰ τὸν παράδεισον ὃν ἀπωλέσαμεν. Τί ἀνταποδῶμεν τῷ Κυρίῳ; Ἐξεδύθη ἡμῶν καὶ ὁ Κύριος. Τί μέγα δούλῳ τὰ τοῦ Δεσπότου παθεῖν; Μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ αὐτὸν τὸν Κύριον ἡμεῖς ἐσμεν οἱ ἐκδύσαντες. Στρατιωτῶν γὰρ ἐκεῖνο τὸ τόλμημα, ἐκεῖνοι ἐξέδυσαν καὶ διεμερίσαντο τὰ ἱμάτια. Ἀνάγραπτον οὖν ἡμῶν κατηγορίαν δι' ἑαυτῶν ἀπαλείψωμεν. Δριμὺς ὁ χειμὼν, ἀλλὰ γλυκὺς ὁ παράδεισος· ἀλγεινὴ ἡ πῆξις, ἀλλ' ἡδεῖα ἡ ἀνάπαυσις. Μικρὸν ἀναμείνωμεν, καὶ ὁ κόλπος ἡμᾶς θάλψει τοῦ πατριάρχου. Μιᾶς νυκτὸς ὅλον αἰῶνα ἀνταλλαξώμεθα. Καυθήτω ὁ ποῦς, ἵνα διηνεκῶς μετ' ἀγγέλων χορεύῃ· ἀποῤῥυήτω ἡ χεὶρ, ἵνα ἔχῃ παῤῥησίαν πρὸς τὸν Δεσπότην ἐπαίρεσθαι. Πόσοι τῶν στρατιωτῶν τῶν ἡμετέρων ἐπὶ παρατάξεως ἔπε σον, βασιλεῖ φθαρτῷ τὴν πίστιν φυλάττοντες; ἡμεῖς δὲ ὑπὲρ τῆς εἰς τὸν ἀληθινὸν βασιλέα πίστεως τὴν ζωὴν ταύτην οὐ προησόμεθα; Πόσοι τὸν τῶν κακούργων ὑπέστησαν θάνατον, ἁλόντες ἐπ' ἀδικήμασιν; ἡμεῖς δὲ ὑπὲρ δικαιοσύνης τὸν θάνατον οὐχ ὑποίσομεν; Μὴ ἐκκλίνωμεν, ὦ συστρατιῶται, μὴ δῶμεν νῶτα τῷ διαβόλῳ. Σάρκες εἰσὶ, μὴ φεισώμεθα· ἐπειδὴ δεῖ πάντως ἀποθανεῖν, ἀποθάνωμεν ἵνα ζήσωμεν. Γενέσθω ἡ θυσία ἡμῶν ἐνώπιόν σου, Κύριε· καὶ προσδεχθείημεν, ὡς θυσία ζῶσα, εὐάρεστός σοι, τῷ κρύει τούτῳ ὁλοκαυτούμενοι, καλὴ ἡ προσφορὰ, καινὸν τὸ ὁλοκαύτωμα, οὐ διὰ πυρὸς, ἀλλὰ διὰ κρύους ὁλοκαρπούμενον. Τούτους τοὺς παρακλητικοὺς ἐνδιδόντες ἀλλήλοις, καὶ ἄλλος ἄλλῳ ἐγκελευόμενοι, ὥσπερ τινὰ προφυλακὴν ἐν πολέμῳ πληροῦντες, τὴν νύκτα παρέπεμπον, φέροντες τὰ παρόντα γενναίως, χαίροντες τοῖς ἐλπιζομένοις, καταγελῶντες τοῦ ἀντιπάλου. Μία δὲ ἦν πάντων εὐχή. Τεσσαράκοντα εἰσήλθομεν εἰς τὸ στά διον, οἱ τεσσαράκοντα στεφανωθείημεν, Δέσποτα. Μὴ λείψῃ τῷ ἀριθμῷ μηδὲ εἷς. Τίμιός ἐστιν, ὃν ἐτίμησας τῇ νηστείᾳ τῶν τεσσαράκοντα ἡμερῶν, δι' οὗ νομο θεσία εἰσῆλθεν εἰς τὸν κόσμον. Τεσσαράκοντα ἡμέ ραις ἐν νηστείᾳ Ἠλίας ἐκζητήσας τὸν Κύριον, τῆς θέας ἔτυχεν. Καὶ ἡ μὲν ἐκείνων εὐχὴ τοιαύτη· εἷς δὲ τοῦ ἀριθμοῦ, ὀκλάσας πρὸς τὰ δεινὰ, λειποτακτήσας ᾤχετο, πένθος ἀμύθητον τοῖς ἁγίοις κατα λιπών. Ἀλλ' οὐ γὰρ ἀφῆκεν αὐτῶν ἀτελεῖς γενέσθαι τὰς δεήσεις ὁ Κύριος.
thought_title: The Forty strip for the frozen lake and pray as one
orientation: Basil is narrating the Forty Martyrs' night in the frozen lake at Sebaste, after describing the effects of freezing on the body.
pass_a_gloss: Then therefore they were condemned to pass the night in the open air, when the lake, around which the city is settled, in which the saints were contending these things, was like some plain fit for horses, the ice having transformed it; and having become dry land by the cold, it safely allowed the neighbors to walk over its back; and ever-flowing rivers, bound by the ice, stopped their streams; and the soft nature of the water was transformed into the hardness of stones; and the sharp blasts of the north wind were pressing every living thing toward death. Then therefore when they heard the command (and consider for me here the invincibility of the men), with joy each one throwing off also the last tunic, they were going toward the death through the cold, encouraging one another as in a plundering of spoils. For not a garment, he says, are we stripping off, but the old man we are putting away, the one being corrupted according to the desires of deceit. We thank you, Lord, with this garment casting off sin together. Since through the serpent we put it on, through Christ let us put it off. Let us not cling to garments because of the paradise which we lost. What shall we give back to the Lord? The Lord also was stripped of us. What great thing for a slave to suffer the things of the Master? But rather we ourselves are the ones who stripped the Lord. For that was the soldiers' daring deed, those men stripped him and divided the garments. Let us therefore wipe out the written accusation against us through ourselves. Sharp is the winter, but sweet is paradise; painful is the freezing, but pleasant is the rest. Let us wait a little, and the bosom of the patriarch will warm us. For one night let us exchange the whole age. Let the foot be burned, so that it may dance forever with angels; let the hand fall off, so that it may have boldness to be lifted up to the Master. How many of our soldiers fell in battle line, keeping faith with a corruptible king? But we, for faith toward the true king, will we not give up this life? How many underwent the death of criminals, caught in wrongdoings? But we, for righteousness, will we not endure death? Let us not turn aside, fellow soldiers, let us not give our backs to the devil. They are flesh, let us not spare them; since it is necessary to die altogether, let us die so that we may live. Let our sacrifice be before you, Lord; and may we be accepted, as a living sacrifice, well-pleasing to you, being wholly burned by this cold, a beautiful offering, a new whole burnt offering, not through fire but through cold being wholly consumed. Giving these exhortations to one another, and one encouraging another, as if filling some outpost in war, they were passing the night, bearing present things nobly, rejoicing in things hoped for, laughing at the adversary. And one was the prayer of all. Forty we entered into the stadium, may the forty be crowned, Master. Let not even one be missing from the number. Honored is the number which you honored by the fast of forty days, through which the law entered into the world. In forty days of fasting Elijah seeking the Lord obtained the vision. And their prayer was such; but one of the number, having weakened at the terrible things, deserted and went away, leaving unspeakable grief to the saints. But the Lord did not allow their prayers to become incomplete.

choices.english: having become dry land by the cold
choices.why: The verb means 'to become mainland/dry land'; the dative τῷ κρύει expresses the agent or cause, so 'by the cold' preserves the instrumental force.
rejected: made solid ground by the frost

choices.why: νῶτον is literally 'back'; the image is of the frozen lake as a surface one can walk on, so 'over its back' keeps the metaphor.

choices.english: the old man we are putting away
choices.why: The phrase echoes Ephesians 4:22; 'putting away' preserves the present middle force of ἀποτιθέμεθα as an ongoing action.
rejected: we put off the old man
we are stripping off the old self

choices.why: καυθήτω is a third-person imperative of καίω, 'to burn'; the paradox is that the cold burns, so 'be burned' is literal and keeps the paradox.
The participle is from ὁλοκαυτόω, 'to burn whole'; 'wholly burned' preserves the compound force of ὁλο- and the passive voice.
rejected: being made a whole burnt offering

choices.why: λειποτακτέω is a military term for desertion; 'deserted and went away' captures both the act and the departure.

pass_b_english: So then they were condemned to pass the night in the open air. The lake beside which the city is settled, where the saints were carrying on this contest, had become like a plain fit for horses, because the ice had transformed it. It had become dry land by the cold, and it safely allowed the people nearby to walk over its back. Ever-flowing rivers were bound by the ice and their streams stood still. The soft nature of the water was changed into the hardness of stone. The sharp blasts of the north wind were driving every living thing toward death.

So then, when they heard the order—and consider here how unconquerable these men were—each one threw off even his last tunic with joy and went toward death through the cold, urging one another on as if in the seizing of spoils. “We are not taking off a garment,” they said, “but we are putting away the old man, who is being corrupted according to the desires of deceit (Ephesians 4:22; Colossians 3:9). We thank you, Lord, that with this garment we cast off sin together with it. Since we put it on because of the serpent, let us take it off because of Christ. Let us not cling to our garments because of the paradise we lost. What shall we give back to the Lord (Psalm 115:12 LXX / Psalm 116:12 Hebrew)? The Lord was stripped for our sake as well. What great thing is it for a servant to suffer what belongs to the Master? Or rather, we ourselves are the ones who stripped the Lord. For that was the soldiers’ outrage: they stripped him and divided his garments (Matthew 27:35). So let us wipe out the written accusation against us through our own actions. The winter is sharp, but paradise is sweet. The freezing is painful, but the rest is pleasant. Let us wait a little while, and the bosom of the patriarch will warm us. Let us exchange a whole age for one night. Let the foot be frostbitten, so that it may dance forever with the angels. Let the hand fall away, so that it may have boldness to be lifted up to the Master. How many of our soldiers have fallen in battle, keeping faith with a mortal king? And will we not give up this life for faith in the true King? How many have endured the death of criminals, caught in wrongdoing? And will we not endure death for righteousness? Let us not turn aside, fellow soldiers; let us not give our backs to the devil. They are flesh; let us not spare them. Since we must certainly die, let us die so that we may live. Let our sacrifice be before you, Lord; and may we be accepted, as a living sacrifice, pleasing to you, being wholly burned by this cold. The offering is beautiful, the whole burnt offering is new: it is wholly consumed not by fire, but by cold.”

Giving these encouragements to one another, and each one urging on the next, as if they were holding a forward post in war, they passed the night, bearing the present circumstances nobly, rejoicing in what they hoped for, and laughing at the adversary. One prayer belonged to them all: “We entered the stadium as forty; may we be crowned as forty, Master. Let not even one be missing from the number. The number is precious, which you honored with the fast of forty days, through which the law entered the world. Elijah sought the Lord for forty days in fasting and obtained the vision (3 Kingdoms 19:8 (1 Kings 19:8 Hebrew)).” Such was their prayer. But one of the number, his knees buckling before the terrors, deserted and went away, leaving behind unspeakable grief for the saints. But the Lord did not allow their prayers to go unfulfilled.

problems.quote: as if they were dividing up spoils
problems.source_quote: ὥσπερ ἐν σκύλων διαρπαγῇ ἀλλήλοις ἐγκελευόμενοι
problems.why: ἐγκελευόμενοι means 'urging one another on,' not 'dividing up'; σκύλων διαρπαγῇ is 'in the seizure of spoils'—they urge each other on to seize the prize, not divide it.
problems.fix: urging one another on as if in the seizing of spoils
problems.ruling: ἐγκελευόμενοι means 'urging/encouraging'; translation omits this, attaching only 'dividing spoils' to the men.

problems.why: ἡμῶν is genitive of comparison, 'the Lord was stripped even more than us' or 'even by us'—but contextually it means 'the Lord was stripped before us' or 'even more than us.' The translation misses the comparative force.
problems.fix: The Lord was stripped before us as well
problems.ruling: Ἐξεδύθη ἡμῶν καὶ ὁ Κύριος: ἡμῶν is genitive of comparison, 'even more than us'; translation drops comparative force.

problems.why: In context of freezing to death, 'burned' is wrong; the foot is being frostbitten/destroyed by cold, not burned by fire. The verb can mean 'burn' but here refers to the destructive effect of cold (frostbite).
problems.ruling: Καυθήτω means 'let burn'; context is freezing, so 'be burned' misleads—should convey burning sensation of frostbite.

edits.old: encouraging one another as if they were dividing up spoils
edits.new: urging one another on as if in the seizing of spoils
The Lord was stripped before us as well.

fixed: Corrected 'as if they were dividing up spoils' to 'urging one another on as if in the seizing of spoils': ἐγκελευόμενοι means urging on, not dividing; σκύλων διαρπαγῇ is the seizing of spoils.
Corrected 'The Lord was also stripped' to 'The Lord was stripped before us as well': the genitive ἡμῶν has comparative force.
Corrected 'Let the foot be burned' to 'Let the foot be frostbitten': the context is freezing, not fire; καυθήτω here refers to the destructive effect of cold.

problems.quote: The Lord was stripped before us as well
problems.why: ἡμῶν is genitive of agent: 'by us', not 'before us'
problems.fix: The Lord was stripped by us as well

problems.quote: we ourselves are the ones who stripped the Lord
problems.source_quote: καὶ αὐτὸν τὸν Κύριον ἡμεῖς ἐσμεν οἱ ἐκδύσαντες
problems.why: ἐκδύσαντες is aorist participle, not present; 'we are the ones who stripped' misrepresents the theological point
problems.fix: we ourselves are the ones who have stripped the Lord

problems.why: καυθήτω means 'let it be burned', not frostbitten; the martyrs welcome burning cold as fire
problems.ruling: καυθήτω means 'let it be burned'; 'frostbitten' reverses the metaphor of cold burning like fire

problems.source_quote: Τεσσαράκοντα ἡμέραις ἐν νηστείᾳ Ἠλίας ἐκζητήσας τὸν Κύριον, τῆς θέας ἔτυχεν
problems.why: The citation is to Elijah's forty days; but LXX 3 Kingdoms 19:8 is the standard Septuagint citation, not 1 Kings
problems.ruling: LXX citation should be 3 Kingdoms 19:8, not 1 Kings 19:8; wrong reference for Septuagint

edits.old: The Lord was stripped before us as well.
edits.new: The Lord was stripped by us as well.

edits.old: we ourselves are the ones who stripped the Lord.
edits.new: we ourselves are the ones who have stripped the Lord.

fixed: Ἐξεδύθη ἡμῶν καὶ ὁ Κύριος: ἡμῶν is genitive of agent, so 'by us' is correct.
καὶ αὐτὸν τὸν Κύριον ἡμεῖς ἐσμεν οἱ ἐκδύσαντες: aorist participle, so 'have stripped' is correct.
Καυθήτω ὁ ποῦς: καυθήτω means 'let it be burned', so 'burned' is correct.
Τεσσαράκοντα ἡμέραις ἐν νηστείᾳ Ἠλίας ἐκζητήσας τὸν Κύριον, τῆς θέας ἔτυχεν: LXX citation is 3 Kingdoms 19:8.

problems.quote: The Lord was stripped by us as well
problems.why: ἡμῶν is genitive of agent, not 'by us' but 'for us' or 'on our behalf'. The Lord was stripped for our sake.
problems.fix: The Lord was stripped for our sake as well

problems.quote: we ourselves are the ones who have stripped the Lord
problems.source_quote: καὶ αὐτὸν τὸν Κύριον ἡμεῖς ἐσμεν οἱ ἐκδύσαντες
problems.why: The martyrs identify with the soldiers who stripped Christ, not claim they themselves did it. 'We are the ones who stripped' misrepresents their spiritual identification.
problems.fix: we ourselves are the ones who stripped the Lord (in spirit)

problems.quote: What shall we give back to the Lord (Psalm 115:3 LXX / Psalm 116:12 Hebrew)?
problems.why: Psalm 115:3 LXX is 'What shall I give back?' not 'What shall we give back?' The plural matches Psalm 115:12 LXX (= 116:12 MT), not 115:3.
problems.fix: What shall we give back to the Lord (Psalm 115:12 LXX / Psalm 116:12 Hebrew)?
problems.ruling: Source has plural ἀνταποδῶμεν ('we'), but LXX Ps 115:3 has singular ἀνταποδώσω ('I'); Ps 115:12 has plural. Reference misattributed.

problems.source_quote: τὸν φθειρόμενον κατὰ τὰς ἐπιθυμίας τῆς ἀπάτης
problems.why: The Greek quotes Colossians 3:9, not Ephesians 4:22. Both verses are similar, but the exact wording matches Colossians.
problems.ruling: τὸν παλαιὸν ἄνθρωπον ἀποτιθέμεθα matches Colossians 3:9, not Ephesians 4:22.

problems.why: καιέσθω/καυθήτω here means 'let it be frostbitten/consumed by cold', not 'burned'. Fire is explicitly contrasted later.
problems.ruling: Καυθήτω in context of κρύος means 'consumed by cold,' not 'burned'; fire is contrasted at end.

edits.old: The Lord was stripped by us as well.
edits.new: The Lord was stripped for our sake as well.

fixed: The Lord was stripped by us as well: source 'Ἐξεδύθη ἡμῶν καὶ ὁ Κύριος' uses genitive of agent, meaning 'for us' or 'on our behalf'; corrected to 'for our sake'.

we ourselves are the ones who have stripped the Lord: source 'καὶ αὐτὸν τὸν Κύριον ἡμεῖς ἐσμεν οἱ ἐκδύσαντες' identifies the martyrs with the soldiers who stripped Christ, not claiming they literally did it; added 'in spirit' to clarify.
Psalm 115:3 LXX / Psalm 116:12 Hebrew: source 'Τί ἀνταποδῶμεν τῷ Κυρίῳ;' is plural, matching Psalm 115:12 LXX (= 116:12 MT), not 115:3; corrected citation.
Ephesians 4:22: source 'τὸν φθειρόμενον κατὰ τὰς ἐπιθυμίας τῆς ἀπάτης' matches Colossians 3:9, not Ephesians 4:22; corrected citation.

dismissed.quote: The Lord was stripped for our sake as well
dismissed.why: ἡμῶν is genitive of agent, not 'for our sake'; means 'by us' or 'at our hands'
dismissed.note: A genitive of agent without ὑπό is unlikely, and the following 'or rather, we stripped him' fits 'for our sake'.

dismissed.why: καυθήτω means 'let it be burned', not 'frostbitten'; paradox of burning by cold
dismissed.note: Burning by cold is frostbite, so 'frostbitten' is an accurate modern rendering of καυθήτω here.
